newsitem.title: INDIA: Frustrated U.S. mulls reward over Kashmir hostages.
newsitem.headline: Frustrated U.S. mulls reward over Kashmir hostages.

text.p: The United States, frustrated over the failure to locate four Western hostages in Kashmir, is considering offering a reward for information about the tourists taken captive 15 months ago, diplomats said on Tuesday.
The money would come from a U.S. government programme that offers up to $2 million for information that can be used to combat acts of "terrorism" aimed at U.S. citizens abroad, they said.
"The purpose is to locate the hostages and apprehend those responsible," a spokesman for the U.S. Embassy in New Delhi said.

Washington has not yet approached India about the idea, and before offering the reward will seek the backing of New Delhi as well as the three other countries whose nationals were kidnapped by separatist guerrillas in mid-1995, diplomats said.
"It's an idea which is being considered," a spokesman for the British High Commission (Embassy) in Delhi said, stressing that no decision had been taken. "Consultations are under way."
Norwegian Ambassador to India Arne Walther said he had no immediate comment on a possible reward. The German Embassy said it would not comment on the hostages.
Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs and Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells were kidnapped by Al-Faran militants while trekking in the Kashmiri mountains on July 4, 1995.
Childs escaped four days later, and Al-Faran captured Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe and German Dirk Hasert. A month later, Ostroe was found beheaded in a remote Kashmiri forest.

Negotiations between Indian officials and Al-Faran broke down last November. Local Kashmiris including nomadic shepherds have periodically reported sighting the four remaining hostages, but authorities have not been able to determine with certainty whether the captives are dead or alive.
Earlier this year, experts using sniffer dogs scoured a forest where a captured militant said he believed the four hostages had been buried. No traces of the men were found.

"Before we move forward, we need the agreement of the quad (British, German, Norwegian) partners and India. We need to feel that all nations involved and the host government agree that this is an effective strategy," the U.S. Embassy spokesman said.
Unknown before the kidnappings, Al-Faran is among dozens of of groups fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir state.

India claims Al-Faran is linked to Pakistan-based Harkat-ul-Ansar and accuses Islamabad of arming and training militants. Pakistan, which rules over one third of Kashmir and has staked a claim to the rest, denies the accusation.

U.S. diplomats said the reward would not amount to ransom as it would not be paid to anyone associated with the kidnappings. "This is not a ransom. There will be no reward paid to those who took part in the kidnappings," a diplomat said.

A diplomat from another Western country said a reward would have to be carefully planned. "Some work needs to be done on it. It could go wrong," the envoy said, citing a demand last year by Al-Faran for a "security deposit" in exchange for the possible release of the hostages.
Officials acknowledged that the idea of a reward reflected a frustration with efforts to locate the hostages and a desire to examine other options.
"We have exhausted every other possibility," the U.S. Embassy spokesman said.
